newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: OPINION-THE CZECH GOVT AND UNIONS, BY JIRI PEHE.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-THE CZECH GOVT AND UNIONS, BY JIRI PEHE.

text.p: Director, Regional Specialists Unit, RFE/RL
PRAGUE, June 24 - The behaviour of Czech trade unions in the next few months may decide the fate of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's besieged government.
The centre-right coalition cabinet is unstable, lacking solid support in parliament and having the trust of only about 20 percent of the potential electorate, according to polls.
The coalition is disjointed, with deputy premier Josef Lux's Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL) increasingly positioning themselves to leave the government at new signs of trouble.
Such problems could emerge, should Czech trade unions decide to fight the government's recently announced package of austerity measures.
Union leaders have been moderate so far, mostly agreeing the country has lived beyond its means and budget cuts are a necessary short-term solution to the current economic problems.
What some unions and the government differ on is what is to cut. The government said it wants to make by far the largest cuts in welfare and social payments. Some unions disagree.
The umbrella Czech and Moravian Chamber of Trade Unions (CMKOS), led by moderate Richard Falbr, has tentatively agreed to tolerate the government's decisions.
However, KOVO, representing steel workers -- the second largest trade union organisation in the country -- has announced it will fight social and welfare payments cuts.
KOVO leaders have said they will wait for the government's concrete decisions but warn they may go on strike in the fall if the government's cuts displease them.
If the government does not change its mind even after such a strike, a general strike will be called.
Nearly all trade unions also disagree with the government's decision to begin the planned liberalisation of energy prices and rents at a time when the budget cuts have to be made.
Should the combined impact of the austerity measures and the price liberalisation prove to be too much for some social groups, trade unions may start protest actions.

Recently the government has done its best to communicate with union leaders. It realises that without at least tacit support from big union organisations, its stabilisation programme, relying on austerity measures, has no chance.
More important, the fragile government has little chance of surviving should a head-on collision with unions take place.
Czech trade unions -- unlike some major unions in Poland and Hungary -- are relatively moderate, in most cases opting for negotiations rather than work stoppages and other protests.

Recent strikes organised by teachers' and railway workers' unions were motivated as much by wage and working conditions demands than by sincere attempts to protest the government's lack of resolve to introduce reforms in those areas.
Trade unionists working in companies seem to have been more aware of problems at the microecomic level than the government.
Analysts working for Falbr's CMKOS warned of possible economic troubles more than a year ago, and proposed solutions.
However, the Klaus government ignored such warnings, just as for a long time it ignored the unions themselves.

The so-called tripartite talks -- involving the government, employers, and trade unions -- were abandoned several years ago, when the government was at the peak of its popularity. Now plans are under way to re-institutionalise such talks.
Falbr told government officials during the recent crown crisis that the main interest of Czech unions was the stability of the currency and the overall stability of the country.
Given the government's past treatment of unions, Falbr could have clearly sought revenge. Instead, he decided to give the government one more chance.

But not all trade union leaders are as moderate as Falbr, who is said to control only one third of trade unions in the country. The limits of his power were apparent in February when railway workers went on strike. Falbr was only partly successful in his attempt to moderate between the government and radical leaders of the railway workers' unions.
The February strike offers some other lessons to the government. First, the government's initial rejections of negotiating with railway workers' leaders backfired because they radicalised the unions.

Second, the government miscalculated in its estimates of what economic loses it can afford. Third, it misjudged the public's reaction to the strike. Most people were angry at railway workers for going on strike over demands that could have been settled by negotiating but, in the end, most people were also critical of the government for its inability to negotiate a quick end to the strike.

Clearly, the Klaus government will need to change its style radically to succeed this time. Some unions are certain to go on strike over social payments cuts. Should the government be unable to seriously discuss concessions, it may easily alienate the entire trade union movement.
Any such development would push the country one step closer to early elections.

(Note - Jiri Pehe is director of the regional analytical unit at Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty based in Prague. The opinions expressed represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.)
